newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Smurfit 1996 profit seen tumbling.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Smurfit 1996 profit seen tumbling.

text.p: Tough times in the paper and packaging industry are expected to take their toll on Jefferson Smurfit Group Plc, leading to a drop of over 50 percent in 1996 pre-tax profits when the company releases its annual results on Tuesday.
Analysts are forecasting pre-tax profits of 200 to 204 million Irish pounds ($320.3 million) compared with 420 million in 1995, a bumper year for the paper industry.
Earnings per share forecasts range from 12.8 to 13.3 pence per share against 28.0 pence a year earlier.
"1995 was the peak year for the paper industry and what you've seen since is some pretty substantial deterioration in the pricing of linerboard," said Joe Burnell, analyst at Davy Stockbrokers.
The average price for linerboard fell to $375 a tonne in 1996 from just over $500 a tonne a year earlier.

"It was down by $130 a tonne which is very significant, a huge reduction in linerboard which accounts over 60 percent of Smurfit's volumes. That was the single most significant factor for Smurfit last year," Burnell said.
But last year's figures are by now academic, analysts say, and the results statement will be closely scrutinised for information on current trading.

Market conditions remain difficult following the industry's failure to push through a $30 price increase in linerboard late last year but analysts say a recovery in prices is possible in the second half of 1997 as the supply/demand situation tightens and excess capacity in the U.S. is absorbed.

"You will get some price recovery in the second half. There's a good possibility of that because what you will see is more mills being taken down because of weak pricing until market conditions improve," said Davy's Burnell.
"The combination of demand and increased downtime will tighten the market so that you will see another attempt by the industry to increase prices at some stage within the next 3-6 months."
But analysts say this will probably come too late to boost the 1997 results.

"You might see some product price movement before the end of the year but it's going to be too late to save 1997," John Conroy, analyst at NCB Stockbrokers, said. "1997 results will definitely be lower than 1996 and will probably be lower than analysts' consensus forecasts."
Another feature of last year's results may be the cash balances, analysts say, as working capital reductions and currency movements help cut debt.

"We believe it will have been a good year for them in terms of debt reduction," says Conroy. "We think debt will be reduced from 586 million to below 500 million, leaving them with gearing of around 35 percent."
Analysts don't expect much movement from the share price, which closed on Friday at 164 Irish pence per share, in the short-term.

"I don't see much downside in it at these levels and equally, it's hard to see it running away with itself until you get very serious confirmation on paper pricing," said David Lowe, analyst at Goodbody Stockbrokers.
